items.description: A look at real weddings and celebrations we've recently covered — captured as they happened, no two moments alike.
items.story:
This isn't one wedding — it's a running album of the ones we've shot most recently, updated as the seasons move. Haldi turmeric mid-air, a groom mid-laugh, a hand caught reaching for another; the kind of frames that only happen once and never get a second take.

We keep this story open on purpose. Every family we work with adds a few more pages to it, and we'd rather show you the real, unedited range of what a House of Echoes wedding actually looks like than a single curated highlight reel.

items.description: A hilltop wedding, a sky that refused to stay one colour, and two families who became one before the sun went down.
items.story:
The venue sat high enough that the ceremony had to work around the wind, not against it — drapes billowing mid-vow, marigolds scattering across the aisle before anyone could stop them. Nobody minded. If anything, it made the whole evening feel less arranged and more alive.

We timed the pheras to chase the light, not the clock, and it paid off: the sky went through gold, then rose, then a deep, bruised purple before the first stars showed up to the reception. Some weddings you plan down to the minute. This one, we just followed.

items.description: No grand stage, no thousand guests — just a courtyard, a few close hearts, and vows that didn't need an audience to matter.
items.story:
Twenty-two guests, a century-old haveli courtyard, and a couple who'd spent months telling us they didn't want anything 'too much.' We took that seriously — no stage, no drone hovering overhead, just low light, close frames, and enough room to actually hear the vows being said.

What we came away with wasn't a smaller wedding film, just a quieter one. The kind where you can hear a grandmother's laugh three rows back, and the bride's hands are shaking just slightly as she says her half of the promise. Some of our favourite frames from this one aren't even during the ceremony — they're the ten minutes before it, when everyone was just standing around, waiting, together.

items.description: A product launch that felt more like a celebration — because the best corporate events aren't about the brand, they're about the people behind it.
items.story:
The brief was simple on paper — cover the launch, get the hero shots of the product on stage, wrap by 10pm. What made the night worth remembering was everything around that brief: the founder pacing backstage rehearsing a line she didn't need to rehearse, the team's genuine reaction when the reveal actually landed, the after-party where the CEO ended up on the dance floor before the caterers had even cleared the first course.

We shoot corporate events the same way we shoot weddings — looking for the unscripted second, not just the keynote slide. That's usually where the best photo in the deck ends up coming from.

items.description: Colours, chants, and a community that's celebrated this festival for generations — we simply made sure it's remembered for one more.
items.story:
This wasn't a private event we were hired into — it was a neighbourhood's festival, running for as many generations as anyone there could count. Our job was to move through it without disrupting it: low to the ground for the processions, close enough for the detail on the hands tying threads, far enough back to let the chanting crowd stay a crowd and not a backdrop.

We came away with more frames of strangers than of anyone we'd been formally introduced to, and that felt right. Cultural coverage, done well, isn't really about any one subject — it's about proving a tradition is still alive, in full colour, this year too.

items.description: A three-day celebration in a palace, captured through candlelit ceremonies, intimate vows, and late-night dance floors.
items.story:
Three days, one palace, and a guest list that flew in from four different countries — this was full-scale destination wedding management from the first vendor call to the last dance floor. We ran the ground logistics alongside the coverage: managing the shot list around the wedding planner's timeline instead of fighting it.

The candlelit sangeet on night one set the tone; by the final night's reception, the whole courtyard was lit end to end and nobody wanted it to be the last song. Our film had to hold three very different moods — reverence, joy, and pure celebration — without any of them feeling like a separate wedding. That balance is the actual craft in a multi-day event like this one.
